primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Dent disease 1 due to CLCN5 loss of function
mechanism: CLCN5 encodes ClC-5, a chloride/proton exchanger localized to proximal tubular subapical endosomes involved in reabsorption of filtered low-molecular-weight proteins. Loss of ClC-5 disrupts endosomal ion handling and proximal tubular protein reabsorption, producing low-molecular-weight proteinuria and commonly hypercalciuria/nephrocalcinosis.
vignette: A 10-year-old boy has recurrent calcium-containing kidney stones. Urinalysis shows marked low-molecular-weight proteinuria and hypercalciuria, and renal ultrasonography shows nephrocalcinosis. His maternal uncle had similar findings. Genetic testing identifies a hemizygous loss-of-function variant in CLCN5.
lead: Which normal function of the affected protein is most directly impaired in this patient?
correct: Chloride/proton exchange in proximal tubular subapical endosomes involved in reabsorption of filtered low-molecular-weight proteins
distractors: Sodium-glucose cotransport across the apical membrane of proximal tubular cells
Cystine export from lysosomes in proximal tubular cells
Electroneutral sodium-chloride cotransport across the apical membrane of distal convoluted tubular cells
Vasopressin-regulated water transport through collecting-duct principal cells
distractor_notes: SGLT-mediated glucose uptake is an apical proximal-tubule process but is not the function of ClC-5 and does not explain the CLCN5-associated phenotype.
Defective lysosomal cystine export is caused by CTNS dysfunction in cystinosis, not CLCN5-related Dent disease.
The thiazide-sensitive Na-Cl cotransporter is encoded by SLC12A3 and functions in the distal convoluted tubule, not proximal-tubule endosomes.
Collecting-duct water permeability is mediated by vasopressin-regulated aquaporin trafficking and is unrelated to ClC-5.
key_expl: Dent disease 1 is caused by CLCN5 variants. ClC-5 is a chloride/proton exchanger in proximal tubular subapical endosomes that supports endosomal handling required for reabsorption of filtered low-molecular-weight proteins.
objective: Link Dent disease 1 to loss of ClC-5-mediated chloride/proton exchange in proximal tubular endosomes.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome is a disorder of lysosome-related organelle biogenesis that causes oculocutaneous albinism and a platelet storage-pool defect with absent platelet delta (dense) granules; PT, PTT, and platelet count are typically normal.
vignette: An 8-year-old child with hypopigmented skin and hair, nystagmus, recurrent epistaxis, and easy bruising has a normal platelet count, prothrombin time, and partial thromboplastin time. Whole-mount electron microscopy of platelets shows absent dense bodies.
lead: Which diagnosis best explains this combination of findings?
distractors: Chediak-Higashi syndrome
Glanzmann thrombasthenia
von Willebrand disease
Isolated oculocutaneous albinism
distractor_notes: Chediak-Higashi syndrome features lysosomal trafficking defects with recurrent infections and giant cytoplasmic granules; absent platelet dense bodies plus the classic HPS phenotype is more specific here.
Glanzmann thrombasthenia is a GPIIb/IIIa platelet aggregation defect and does not cause oculocutaneous albinism.
von Willebrand disease can cause mucocutaneous bleeding but does not cause albinism or absent platelet delta granules.
Isolated oculocutaneous albinism does not explain the platelet dense-granule storage-pool defect and bleeding diathesis.
key_expl: Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome combines oculocutaneous albinism with a bleeding diathesis caused by absent platelet delta granules; platelet count and routine coagulation times are typically normal.
objective: Recognize Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome from the combination of albinism, mucocutaneous bleeding, and absent platelet dense bodies.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
Hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies (HNPP)
mechanism: HNPP is usually caused by a recurrent deletion involving PMP22 that reduces PMP22 dosage. PMP22 haploinsufficiency disrupts peripheral myelin and predisposes to recurrent focal neuropathies after compression or minor trauma.
vignette: A 27-year-old man has had several episodes of transient foot drop and hand numbness after prolonged leg crossing or leaning on his elbows. His father has a similar history. Nerve conduction studies show a demyelinating peripheral neuropathy, and chromosomal microarray identifies a recurrent deletion at 17p11.2 involving PMP22.
lead: Which molecular consequence most directly causes this patient's disorder?
correct: PMP22 haploinsufficiency from reduced gene dosage
distractors: Increased PMP22 gene dosage from a reciprocal duplication
Gain-of-function mutation of a neuronal voltage-gated sodium channel
Loss of dystrophin-mediated linkage between actin and the extracellular matrix
Defective mitochondrial fusion caused by biallelic loss of MFN2
distractor_notes: A reciprocal PMP22-containing duplication at this locus is associated with Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1A rather than HNPP.
Neuronal sodium-channel gain-of-function causes channelopathies such as some epilepsy or pain syndromes, not the recurrent pressure palsy phenotype produced by PMP22 deletion.
Dystrophin deficiency causes Duchenne/Becker muscular dystrophy rather than a compression-sensitive demyelinating neuropathy.
MFN2 variants are associated with axonal Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease and are not the molecular consequence of the PMP22 deletion shown.
key_expl: HNPP is a PMP22 dosage disorder. The recurrent 17p11.2 deletion produces PMP22 haploinsufficiency, reducing peripheral myelin protein 22 and predisposing nerves to focal demyelination after pressure.
objective: Associate HNPP with reduced PMP22 gene dosage and haploinsufficiency.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: ALPL encodes tissue-nonspecific alkaline phosphatase (TNSALP), a membrane-bound ectophosphatase whose natural substrates include inorganic pyrophosphate. Reduced TNSALP activity causes hypophosphatasia with low serum alkaline phosphatase and defective bone and dental mineralization.
vignette: A 6-year-old child has premature loss of several primary incisors with intact roots and radiographs showing undermineralized bone. Serum alkaline phosphatase activity is repeatedly below the age-adjusted reference range. A pathogenic variant in ALPL is identified.
lead: Loss of which normal enzymatic activity most directly reflects the affected gene product?
correct: Hydrolysis of extracellular inorganic pyrophosphate by tissue-nonspecific alkaline phosphatase
distractors: Hydroxylation of proline residues during collagen synthesis
Cleavage of type I collagen amino-terminal propeptides
Conversion of 25-hydroxyvitamin D to 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D
Carbonic anhydrase-mediated generation of protons in osteoclasts
distractor_notes: Prolyl hydroxylation is required for collagen maturation but is not the function of ALPL/TNSALP.
Type I procollagen processing defects cause other skeletal dysplasias and do not account for low alkaline phosphatase from ALPL dysfunction.
Renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase activates vitamin D but is not encoded by ALPL.
Osteoclast carbonic anhydrase supports bone resorption; hypophosphatasia is caused by deficient TNSALP ectophosphatase activity.
key_expl: ALPL encodes TNSALP, a membrane-bound ectophosphatase. Inorganic pyrophosphate is one of its natural substrates; loss of TNSALP activity produces low alkaline phosphatase and defective bone/tooth mineralization.
objective: Link hypophosphatasia to loss of ALPL-encoded tissue-nonspecific alkaline phosphatase activity toward inorganic pyrophosphate.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Andersen-Tawil syndrome is a channelopathy, often related to KCNJ2, characterized by the triad of episodic flaccid weakness (periodic paralysis), ventricular arrhythmias/prominent U waves, and distinctive dysmorphic features.
vignette: A 16-year-old adolescent has recurrent episodes of flaccid limb weakness after prolonged rest. ECG between episodes shows frequent ventricular ectopy with prominent U waves. Examination shows low-set ears, a small mandible, and clinodactyly.
lead: Which diagnosis best explains this constellation of findings?
distractors: Catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia
Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis
Long QT syndrome due to KCNQ1 dysfunction
Brugada syndrome
distractor_notes: CPVT produces exercise- or catecholamine-triggered ventricular arrhythmias but does not characteristically combine periodic paralysis with the dysmorphic phenotype and prominent U waves of Andersen-Tawil syndrome.
Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis can cause episodic weakness but does not explain the characteristic ventricular ectopy, prominent U waves, and dysmorphic features.
KCNQ1-related long QT syndrome causes repolarization abnormalities but not the classic triad of periodic paralysis, ventricular arrhythmias, and dysmorphism.
Brugada syndrome produces a characteristic right-precordial ST-segment pattern and ventricular arrhythmia risk, not this multisystem triad.
key_expl: Andersen-Tawil syndrome is recognized by episodic flaccid weakness, ventricular arrhythmias with prominent U waves or prolonged QU intervals, and characteristic dysmorphic features.
objective: Recognize the characteristic neuromuscular, cardiac, and dysmorphic triad of Andersen-Tawil syndrome.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis type 2 (BSEP deficiency) due to ABCB11 dysfunction
mechanism: ABCB11 encodes the bile salt export pump (BSEP), an ATP-binding cassette transporter on the canalicular membrane of hepatocytes that mediates biliary bile-acid export. BSEP deficiency causes PFIC2 with cholestasis and typically low or normal GGT.
vignette: An infant develops progressive jaundice and intense pruritus. Laboratory studies show conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with elevated aminotransferases but low gamma-glutamyl transferase activity. Genetic testing identifies biallelic pathogenic variants in ABCB11.
lead: Which hepatocyte transport process is most directly impaired?
correct: ATP-dependent export of bile salts across the canalicular membrane into bile
distractors: Sodium-dependent uptake of bile salts across the basolateral membrane from portal blood
Canalicular secretion of conjugated bilirubin by MRP2
Canalicular export of phosphatidylcholine by MDR3
Basolateral export of bile acids from hepatocytes back into sinusoidal blood
distractor_notes: Basolateral sodium-dependent bile-salt uptake is mediated principally by NTCP, not ABCB11/BSEP.
MRP2 transports conjugated bilirubin and other organic anions; it is distinct from BSEP-mediated bile-salt export.
MDR3/ABCB4 exports phosphatidylcholine and is associated with PFIC3, which typically has elevated GGT.
Basolateral bile-acid efflux is a compensatory route in cholestasis but is not the normal canalicular BSEP function lost in PFIC2.
key_expl: ABCB11 encodes BSEP, the major canalicular bile-salt exporter. Loss of BSEP impairs ATP-dependent secretion of bile salts from hepatocytes into bile and produces PFIC2, often with low or normal GGT.
objective: Link ABCB11-related PFIC2 to impaired canalicular bile-salt export by BSEP.

outline: Resistance to thyroid hormone beta / THRB
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Resistance to thyroid hormone beta (RTHβ) due to THRB dysfunction
mechanism: RTHβ is caused by impaired thyroid hormone receptor beta signaling. Reduced tissue sensitivity to thyroid hormone, including impaired pituitary feedback, permits persistently elevated free thyroid hormone concentrations with nonsuppressed TSH.
vignette: A 20-year-old patient has repeatedly elevated free thyroxine and triiodothyronine concentrations with a nonsuppressed thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration. The patient is clinically stable, takes no interfering medications, and has no pituitary mass on imaging. A heterozygous pathogenic variant in THRB is identified.
lead: Which physiologic abnormality most directly explains this laboratory pattern?
correct: Reduced thyroid hormone receptor beta-mediated negative feedback on pituitary TSH secretion
distractors: Constitutive activation of the TSH receptor in thyroid follicular cells
Destruction of thyroid follicles with release of preformed thyroid hormone
Loss of thyroid peroxidase activity causing impaired organification of iodide
Excess somatostatin release causing suppression of pituitary TSH secretion
distractor_notes: Constitutive TSH-receptor activation causes autonomous thyroid hormone production with suppression of TSH, not a nonsuppressed TSH.
Destructive thyroiditis releases preformed hormone but ordinarily suppresses TSH through intact negative feedback.
Thyroid peroxidase deficiency reduces thyroid hormone synthesis and tends to raise TSH rather than produce high free T4/T3 with nonsuppressed TSH from hormone resistance.
Somatostatin suppresses TSH and cannot explain a nonsuppressed TSH in the presence of elevated free thyroid hormones.
key_expl: RTHβ reflects impaired responsiveness to thyroid hormone from THRB dysfunction. Pituitary feedback is blunted, so TSH is not appropriately suppressed despite elevated circulating free thyroid hormone.
objective: Recognize the feedback physiology of THRB-related resistance to thyroid hormone beta.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Primary hyperoxaluria type 1 due to AGXT deficiency
mechanism: AGXT encodes liver peroxisomal alanine-glyoxylate aminotransferase (AGT), which converts glyoxylate to glycine. Loss of AGT causes glyoxylate accumulation and conversion to oxalate, leading to calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis and nephrocalcinosis.
vignette: A 9-year-old child has recurrent calcium oxalate kidney stones and nephrocalcinosis with markedly increased urinary oxalate excretion. Genetic testing identifies biallelic pathogenic variants in AGXT.
lead: Which metabolic reaction is most directly impaired?
correct: Peroxisomal transamination of glyoxylate to glycine
distractors: Mitochondrial oxidation of homogentisate to maleylacetoacetate
Cytosolic conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine
Lysosomal degradation of globotriaosylceramide
Mitochondrial conversion of methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA
distractor_notes: Homogentisate metabolism is impaired in alkaptonuria and is unrelated to AGXT-dependent glyoxylate detoxification.
Phenylalanine hydroxylation is impaired in phenylketonuria, not primary hyperoxaluria type 1.
Globotriaosylceramide degradation is impaired in Fabry disease and does not generate the oxalate phenotype.
Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase deficiency causes methylmalonic acidemia, not calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis from AGT loss.
key_expl: AGT is a liver peroxisomal enzyme encoded by AGXT that converts glyoxylate to glycine. In PH1, reduced AGT activity diverts accumulated glyoxylate toward oxalate production.
objective: Link primary hyperoxaluria type 1 to impaired peroxisomal conversion of glyoxylate to glycine by AGT.

mechanism: Partial verification bias occurs in diagnostic-accuracy studies when only a selected, nonrandom subset of participants who received the index test undergoes the reference standard, often because the index-test result influences who is verified.
vignette: Investigators evaluate a new blood test for pancreatic cancer. All 1,200 participants receive the index test, but only participants with a positive index test undergo the reference-standard biopsy. The investigators then estimate diagnostic accuracy using only participants whose disease status was verified.
lead: Which bias most directly threatens the reported diagnostic accuracy?
distractors: Incorporation bias
Diagnostic review bias
Spectrum bias
Lead-time bias
distractor_notes: Incorporation bias occurs when the index test itself is incorporated into the reference standard used to define disease, which is not described here.

Diagnostic review bias occurs when interpretation of the reference standard is influenced by knowledge of the index-test result; the central defect here is selective performance of the reference standard.
Spectrum bias concerns differences in the clinical spectrum of participants compared with the target population, not selective verification based on index-test results.
Lead-time bias affects apparent survival after earlier diagnosis and is not a diagnostic-accuracy verification problem.
key_expl: Only index-test-positive participants receive the reference standard, so verification is nonrandom and depends on the index test. This is partial verification bias, also called work-up bias.
objective: Identify partial verification bias when the reference standard is applied only to a selected subset after an index test.
clues: only index-positive participants receive reference standard

system: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
outline: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
mechanism: Teach-back is an evidence-based health-literacy communication technique in which the patient or caregiver explains in their own words what they need to know or do, allowing the clinician to confirm that information was explained clearly and understood.
vignette: A physician explains a new home medication schedule to a patient with limited health literacy. Before ending the visit, the physician says, “I want to be sure I explained this clearly. Please tell me in your own words how you will take these medicines when you get home.”
lead: Which communication technique is the physician using?
distractors: Motivational interviewing
Shared decision-making
Closed-loop communication during team resuscitation
Formal assessment of decision-making capacity
distractor_notes: Motivational interviewing elicits a patient's motivations and resolves ambivalence; it is not defined by asking the patient to restate instructions in their own words.
Shared decision-making integrates evidence with the patient's preferences when choosing among options; the scenario is checking comprehension of already-explained instructions.
Closed-loop team communication confirms receipt and completion of an order among team members; the described patient-centered comprehension check is teach-back.
Decision-making capacity assessment evaluates understanding, appreciation, reasoning, and ability to express a choice; this brief health-literacy technique is not a capacity evaluation.
key_expl: Teach-back asks the patient or caregiver to explain information or required actions in their own words. It verifies the clarity of the clinician's explanation and the patient's understanding better than simply asking whether the patient understands.
objective: Recognize teach-back as the preferred technique for confirming patient understanding of health information.
clues: clinician frames it as checking own explanation
patient asked to repeat plan in own words
